title: When to Leap
subtitle: In the mid-1990s a technology analyst drew a curve on a whiteboard to explain why every new technology seems first a miracle, then a disappointment — and only later useful.

card.essence: Excitement about a new technology rises far faster than the technology itself. After the peak comes a fall — and only those that survive the fall become part of everyday life.

intention: you'll learn how the hype cycle was born and what the evidence says about it, place real technologies on the curve, and practise the future in the past: It was going to change everything. Experts said it would …
warmup: Think of a new technology everyone was excited about. Did it live up to the excitement?
Are you usually an early adopter, or do you wait until something is proven?
Why do you think the media loves to announce “the next big thing”?

vocab.heading: A · What do they mean here? Work it out from the context
vocab.intro: Read the sentence, guess the meaning of the word in bold, then reveal.

items.sent: The film had so much hype before it came out that the reality was bound to disappoint.
items.meaning: hype — excited, exaggerated publicity. (media hype; overhyped; verb hype something up)

items.sent: House prices reached their peak in the spring and then started to fall.
items.meaning: peak — the highest point. (reach a peak; peak season; peak hours)

items.sent: After two years of broken promises, there was widespread disillusionment with the new government.
items.meaning: disillusionment — the disappointment you feel when something is not as good as you believed. (adj. disillusioned)

items.sent: Sales fell to a trough in January, then slowly recovered.
items.meaning: trough — a low point between two higher points. (pronounced /trɒf/; peaks and troughs)

vocab.heading: B · Which word matches the meaning?
vocab.intro: The three words are: plateau · breakthrough · bubble. Read each meaning, say the word, then reveal.

items.sent: (noun) An important discovery or development that suddenly makes progress possible.
(noun) A situation where prices or excitement rise far above real value, and then suddenly collapse.
items.meaning: bubble — “When the bubble burst, the shares were worth almost nothing.”

items.sent: (noun) A period when something stays at the same level after a time of rising.
items.meaning: plateau — “After a year of fast progress, my Spanish reached a plateau.”

vocab.heading: C · Which word completes all three phrases?
vocab.intro: One missing word fits every phrase in the group. Say it, then reveal.

items.meaning: inflated — bigger than it should be. (verb inflate; noun inflation)

items.sent: ___ a new technology  ·  ___ a child  ·  ___ a strategy
items.meaning: adopt — to start using something; or to legally take a child into your family. (noun adoption; an early adopter)

items.sent: ___ up to the hype  ·  ___ up to expectations  ·  ___ up to your promises
items.meaning: live — live up to something = be as good as people expected or as you promised.

vocab_use: What's the most overhyped product or film you remember?
Have you ever felt disillusioned with a job, a course or an app? What happened?
Are you an early adopter? Give an example.

story.heading: Part 1 — A curve on a whiteboard
paras: In 1994 Jackie Fenn joined Gartner, a company that advises businesses about technology. The World Wide Web was just moving from a research curiosity to a global phenomenon, and part of her job was to judge which new technologies would really matter.

Looking back at earlier waves — artificial intelligence, genetic engineering, personal computers — she saw the same pattern again and again: a flood of excitement, then disappointment when the technology failed to live up to it, and only later real, useful adoption. She sketched the shape on a whiteboard.

In 1995 she published it in a research note called “When to Leap on the Hype Cycle”. Its advice was practical: “Organizations should select the optimal time to begin investing in a new technology by matching their risk tolerance against a technology's progress along the hype cycle.”
checks: What was part of Fenn's job at Gartner?
answers: To judge which new technologies would really matter.
Excitement, then disappointment, then real and useful adoption.
To choose when to invest by matching how much risk you can accept to where the technology is on the curve.
story.discuss: Why do people get so excited about new technologies before they work properly?

story.heading: Part 2 — Peaks and troughs
paras: Fenn expected it to be a one-off. But the following year, clients asked for an update with the latest technologies. In the 1996 version, the peak of the curve featured Java, internet terminals and the World Wide Web. Hype cycles became a regular Gartner report.

The curve has five named stages. A breakthrough — the innovation trigger — starts the story. Publicity climbs to the peak of inflated expectations. When early products fail to deliver, interest falls into the trough of disillusionment. Slowly, people work out what the technology is really good for: the slope of enlightenment. Finally comes the plateau of productivity, when it is simply used.
The names were memorable enough to escape. The term “hype cycle” and its stages are now used far beyond Gartner, in the marketing of all kinds of new technologies.
checks: Why did Fenn update the curve in 1996?
What was at the peak in 1996?
Name the five stages in order.
answers: Because clients asked for an update.
Java, internet terminals and the World Wide Web.
Innovation trigger, peak of inflated expectations, trough of disillusionment, slope of enlightenment, plateau of productivity.
story.discuss: Which technology do you think is at the peak right now?

story.heading: Part 3 — Is it even a cycle?
paras: The hype cycle has its critics. It is not really a cycle, they point out, and it is not scientific: there is little data to prove that technologies actually follow it. Its stages are named after feelings — expectations, disillusionment, enlightenment — which makes it hard to say where a technology really is.

In 2024 The Economist tested the idea against years of Gartner's own reports. It concluded that only a small share of technologies — perhaps a fifth — moved from innovation to excitement to despair to widespread use. And of the technologies that fell into the trough, it estimated, six in ten never rose again.

Fenn herself has said the danger is people being “reactive to the hype cycle, so they're rushing in when the hype's up and abandoning it when the hype's down again.” Perhaps the curve's best use is not as a prediction at all, but as a warning about ourselves.
checks: Give two criticisms of the hype cycle.
What did Fenn say the danger was?
answers: Any two: it isn't really a cycle; it isn't scientific — there's little data behind it; its stages are named after feelings, so it's hard to place technologies.
That perhaps only a fifth of technologies follow the whole curve, and six in ten of those in the trough never recover.
People rushing in when the hype is up and giving up when it's down.
story.discuss: If most technologies don't follow the curve, is it still useful?

tool_tab.lead: The curve shows expectations over time — not how good the technology really is. The gap between the two is where the money, and the mistakes, are made.
how: Name the technology, and be specific: “electric scooters for hire in cities”, not just “transport”.
Ask where expectations are now: is everyone talking about it, or has the excitement faded?
Separate the talk from the evidence: who is actually using it, and is it working for them?
Decide your move: leap early (high risk), wait for the slope, or ignore it — and remember that many technologies never complete the curve.

sort.intro: Here are six moments in the life of an imaginary technology — home robots. Which stage of the curve does each one describe?

items.text: Robot companies go bankrupt, and newspapers ask: “Whatever happened to home robots?”
A university lab shows a video of a robot folding laundry. There is no product yet.
A second generation of robots does just three jobs well, and some hotels start using them.
items.why: people are learning what it is really good for.

items.text: Every magazine cover promises that by next year, nobody will do housework.
Home robots are boring now: they're in millions of homes, and nobody writes about them.
Investors pour money into fifty start-ups, although few of them have sold a single robot.
items.why: money follows the excitement, not the results.

breaks: It isn't a law. Many technologies don't follow the full curve, and some never come back from the trough.
Feelings, not facts. Expectations are hard to measure, so placing a technology on the curve is a judgement.
It can become an excuse. “It's just in the trough” can be said about a technology that has simply failed.
discuss: Place three real technologies on the curve. Does your teacher agree?
When did you last rush in too early — or give up too soon?

grammar.name: the future in the past: was going to, would
grammar.lead: Hype is full of predictions — and later we look back on them. To talk about the future as it looked from the past, English uses was/were going to, would and was/were supposed to.
notes:
was / were going to + base verb — a plan or prediction in the past, often one that didn't happen.
“We were going to buy a house, but prices rose.”

would + base verb — the past form of will, especially after said, thought, believed, promised.
“She promised she would call.”  “Everyone thought the shop would close.”

was / were supposed to + base verb — what was expected or arranged, usually with disappointment.
“The train was supposed to arrive at six.”

was / were about to + base verb — something that was going to happen very soon.
“I was about to leave when the phone rang.”
Watch out: after a past reporting verb, will usually becomes would: ~~They said it will be easy~~ → “They said it would be easy.”

exercises.heading: Complete the predictions
exercises.intro: Use the verbs in brackets with would, was/were going to or was/were supposed to. More than one answer may be possible.
items: 1. The company promised that the new phone ___ (last) a whole week on one charge.
2. We ___ (launch) the app in May, but the tests went badly.
3. The robots ___ (do) all the housework, but they couldn't even climb the stairs.
4. Everyone thought the shares ___ (keep) rising for ever.
5. I ___ (buy) one, but then I read the reviews.
answers: 3. were supposed to do (or were going to do)

exercises.heading: Report the promises
exercises.intro: Rewrite each prediction as a sentence about the past, starting with the words given.
items: 1. “This technology will change everything.” → Experts said ___
2. “We are going to sell a million units.” → The company announced that it ___
3. “It will be in every home within five years.” → Magazines predicted that it ___
4. “The price will fall soon.” → We thought ___
answers: 2. …was going to sell a million units.
3. …would be in every home within five years.

grammar.closing: Now tell your teacher about something you were going to do this year but haven't — and something you thought would happen but didn't.

speak.intro: Talk about hype — and about your own reactions to it. Choose a task, start the timer, and talk.
speak.useful: “Everyone said it would …” · “It was supposed to …, but …” · “I think it's at the peak right now.” · “It's climbing the slope.”

tasks.label: Task 1 — On the curve
paras: Choose three technologies you know — from electric cars to an app on your phone. Place each one on the curve and explain why.

tasks.label: Task 2 — Your own hype cycle
paras: Describe something you were very excited about — a job, a hobby, a city — that disappointed you. Did you later find its real value?

tasks.label: Task 3 — Leap or wait?
paras: Your company wants to invest in a new technology. Argue for leaping early, or for waiting.

final: Is hype necessary? Would new technologies get any money without it?
Who benefits most from the peak of inflated expectations?
If many technologies never leave the trough, how can we tell a slow success from a real failure?
From memory: tell the story of one imaginary flop using was going to, would and was supposed to.
